02 / Hackathon project

AllAbout Campus

A web-agent demo our team built at the Battle of Schools Hackathon. You ask a U of T or Waterloo question; it reads relevant pages, answers with citations, and lists the sources it could not check.

OverviewEngineeringResults & evidence
Role
Team lead, team of four
When
Sep 2026
Stack
React, TypeScript, Fastify, Steel SDK, Playwright
Status
Hackathon demo

What I did

  • Team leadership: Rui, Yilin, Ziqin and I built it. I set the plan and led backend work with the team.
  • Implementation: I connected the frontend, backend and browser flow and worked on source routing, evidence extraction and coverage reporting.
  • Delivery: I added preflight and regression checks, reviewed the frontend and presented the final demo, recorded for YouTube.
  • Repository on GitHub

The problem

Answers to course and campus questions are spread across university sites, calendars and pages behind a login. An answer is only useful if the student can see where it came from and which pages were never checked.

What the interface shows
  • Course Desk. The question panel, with shortcuts for course desk, timetable and assessments, and sample questions for a course.
  • Browser view. The Steel Live Browser panel shows pages as the agent reads them, and you can step back through them afterwards.
  • Citations. The answer links to the pages it relied on.
  • Coverage receipt. A record of which sources were checked, and which were inaccessible or did not contain enough evidence, so gaps are visible rather than hidden.

From question to evidence

University pages and community discussion are labelled separately. A captured page is not automatically evidence for a claim: the quoted text must support the answer and match its course and term. API failures stop the live path instead of silently substituting a keyword-based answer.

A source-routing regression

General course questions were being mixed with a Timetable Builder source that did not answer them. This diluted the evidence path. We changed general CSC207 and CSC148 routing to the Academic Calendar and Computer Science department, and removed the irrelevant source from the registry, interface labels, coverage catalogue and smoke-test target.

The important change was consistency across those layers: removing a source from the collector alone would still leave misleading coverage expectations in the interface and tests.

Live, fixture and login-only sources
Live browsing
For public questions, OpenAI web search finds up to three relevant pages and Steel reads their content. This needs configured API access.
Fixture demo
Repeatable runs from prepared data, labelled in the interface (“Demo sources”, “Simulated browsing”). Used for presenting, not as live research.
Login required
The repository has Quercus and ACORN adapters and a login flow for private course material. I found no record confirming a real-account run during the hackathon. When a source can't be accessed, the coverage receipt says so.

Result and status

A repeatable hackathon demo, still in development. Its fixture replay shows how an updated deadline supersedes an older one and how an unanswered question stays visible. Tests check routing and evidence contracts; they do not establish that every answer is correct. I found no record confirming a real-account Quercus or ACORN run during the hackathon. How sources are handled

Recorded fixture run

Checks

Preflight and regression checks cover routing, browser execution, cancellation, cleanup and evidence integration, so the public demo could be rerun reliably.

Limits

This is a hackathon demo, not a university information service. The checks cover how the pipeline behaves, not whether answers are correct, and a cited answer can still miss a relevant rule or page. We are still developing it, including the login-based sources.
